title: Tuscaloosa tornado damage
description: Package about a Class 5 tornado causing damage to Armed Forces Reserve Center and AMSA shop. alatornado11, tornado11

transcript.text: Despite its appearance, this is not a war zone.
On April 27, the 81st RSC's ANSA Shop 154 and the Armed Forces Reserve Center suffered major damage as a Category 5 tornado devastated the west central town of Tuscaloosa, Alabama.
Hardest hit was the ANSA Shop and its motor pool, incurring losses to the 81st RSC that are expected to reach as much as $10 million.

With winds in excess of 190 miles per hour, the tornado tore off sections of the roof, toppled five-ton trucks, impaled vehicles with projectile debris, and even had one shop worker trapped inside the building who fortunately escaped harm.

Staff Sergeant Keltner Patterson, a refrigeration specialist with the 75th Combat Support Hospital, is also a military technician who was working his civilian job as a heavy equipment repairman with the ANSA Shop when the twisters dropped.

We had a Category 5 tornado to come through Tuscaloosa right over this shop. I got trapped in, couldn't get out, couldn't get to a safe place, and this was the safest place that I could be at at the time.

Where did you go? What did you do? I went into the building here behind me, went to the bathroom and got on the lowest part into a corner between a door facing there, and that's why I survived the storm.

It is estimated that damages to the motor pool alone will reach a quarter of a million dollars. Sergeant First Class Jimmy Orange, the 75th Cash Motor Pool Sergeant, explained what he needs to do next.

They're going to come Monday, and this third, the second of May, they're going to ship these vehicles out to two-ounce the shop, and they're going to have an answer personnel down there and do all that assessment.
And then they're going to fix them at two shops, one in Meridian and one in Tubalomissant.
Inside the Reserve Center, the entrance doors were blown out, display cases were thrown around, and even fire doors were torn off their hinges.
Now, in the aftermath of all the destruction, safety and security of the soldiers and facilities is the number one priority for Major Michael Kaufman.
Basically, we have a presence here, and there's a police presence locally. The building's not safe to occupy.
All of our equipment that is considered sensitive has been relocated to another facility.
Most of the remaining equipment and documentation is just standard issue equipment that would not require any additional level of security.

We do have, again, a presence here, 24-7, to guard the perimeter in the facility, but again, it's not a very safe location to have people inside the building in the evening hours with no power and some of the damage to the facility.
Have there been any instances of looting that you've heard of?
None that I'm aware of.
Okay. Do you expect her to use her CNE?

Do not for CNE. In fact, I know that the AD-1RRC is in the process of looking at establishing a new perimeter fence line, which will resecure the facility and won't require a need for a 24-hour presence.
The civilians and soldiers in Tuscaloosa have a long road ahead of them in order to get things cleaned up.
But rest assured that these Wildcats will never quit.
Reporting from Tuscaloosa, I'm Gail Anderson, AD-1RSC.
